subsection: 6. The Western economies, 1945–1973: growth, Marshall Aid, free trade, immigration and the welfare state

notes.h: Background: war, depression and the Western economic model
notes.b: To understand the post-war boom you need to know what Europe was recovering from and what its governments were determined to avoid. They rebuilt a capitalist system, but one with a much bigger role for the state than before the war.
points: The Second World War ended in 1945 with much of Europe in ruins, while the USA emerged as the leading economy in the world. From 1947 the Cold War (the hostile standoff between the USA and the Soviet Union) began to divide Europe.

Post-war planners remembered the inter-war years: the Great Depression, protectionism (high tariffs to keep foreign goods out) and mass unemployment. Governments wanted growth, open trade and full employment so that this would not happen again.

Capitalism means private ownership, competitive markets and profit. Western Europe stayed capitalist, in contrast to communism, but ran a mixed economy, with state planning, nationalisation (state ownership of key industries) and welfare provision.
The welfare state means the state provides health care, pensions, unemployment benefit and education, paid for through taxation and insurance contributions.
A common market means free movement of goods, services, capital and workers inside a group of countries, with a common external tariff (the same import tax on goods from outside the group).
notes.tip: Define welfare state, capitalism and common market in a sentence each as they apply to 1945–1973.

notes.h: Post-war devastation and the need for recovery
notes.b: Western Europe emerged from the war with damaged cities, disrupted trade and food shortages, which made reconstruction the first priority. Its weakness also made the USA's economic and political help decisive.
points: Much of the industrial capacity of Germany, France and Italy was damaged or destroyed, and transport networks, bridges and ports had to be rebuilt before trade could restart.
Food and fuel were scarce, so rationing continued in several countries into the late 1940s.
The winter of 1946–47 was exceptionally severe. Coal and fuel shortages slowed factories and transport across Western Europe, including British and continental industry.
Europe suffered from a dollar gap: it needed American goods, such as food and machinery, but had no dollars to pay for them, so it ran a large trade deficit with the USA.

Britain borrowed heavily from the USA, including an Anglo-American loan of about 3.75 billion dollars agreed in December 1945. It stayed dependent on dollars and devalued the pound from 4.03 dollars to 2.80 dollars in September 1949.

Several million German refugees and expellees from the east settled in West Germany by the early 1950s. At first they were a burden because they worsened housing shortages, but they later supplied labour for industry.

The Cold War shaped recovery. In 1947 France and Italy had strong communist parties, and American leaders feared that poverty would increase their support, so the Marshall Plan aimed to prevent economic collapse from strengthening communism.
notes.tip: If asked why Europe needed American aid, name the dollar gap and give the Britain example: the 1945 loan and the 1949 devaluation.

notes.h: Marshall Aid: the offer and how it worked
notes.b: The USA offered large-scale aid to rebuild Western Europe, partly out of generosity but mainly to bring stability and block the spread of communism. The aid came with conditions that pushed European states to work together.
points: US Secretary of State George Marshall offered aid in a speech at Harvard on 5 June 1947. The Soviet Union refused and pressed its satellites (the states under its control) to refuse, and Molotov left the Paris talks in July 1947.

Sixteen states took part in the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), set up on 16 April 1948, and received aid. Recipients had to draw up plans for recovery, and the OEEC coordinated the allocation of aid.

The Economic Cooperation Act passed in April 1948. The European Recovery Programme ran from 1948 to 1952 and provided about 13 billion dollars, mostly as grants, which means money that did not have to be repaid.
The largest recipients were Britain, France and West Germany. Aid paid for food, fuel, raw materials and machinery, which helped solve the dollar gap.
Counterpart funds were local currency raised by selling the American goods inside each country. Governments used them to finance investment in industry and housing.
The OEEC later became the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in 1961, when the USA and Canada joined. Do not confuse the OEEC with the EEC.
notes.tip: For a short answer on Marshall Aid, give dated statements: the speech of June 1947, the programme of 1948–52, about 13 billion dollars and grants rather than loans.

notes.h: Marshall Aid: conditions, the EPU and its impact
notes.b: Marshall Aid was meant to do more than supply dollars. It tied recipients to cooperation and to open trade, and historians still argue about how much it really achieved.
points: Aid was linked to conditions: removing trade barriers, controlling inflation and keeping finances stable. This pushed European states away from the protectionism of the 1930s.

The European Payments Union of 1950 introduced multilateral clearing of members' trade balances. In other words, countries settled their trade accounts together instead of one pair at a time, which helped to revive trade between members.
Aid also promoted American-style productivity methods, such as more efficient factory organisation and management.
Aid gave the USA political leverage. It was meant to strengthen stability and weaken communism's appeal, which fits the American policy of containment (stopping the spread of communism).
The historian Alan Milward, in The Reconstruction of Western Europe, 1945–51 (1984), argued that aid was a modest share of national investment and that domestic policy mattered more.

The case for aid is that it supplied dollars and confidence when Europe was short of both. The case against is that its money was a small part of total investment, so recovery depended mostly on European effort.
notes.tip: Examiners want Marshall Aid and free trade compared: show how aid worked (grants, OEEC, counterpart funds), its limits, and how GATT, the EPU, the ECSC, the EEC and EFTA built on it.

notes.h: Bretton Woods and GATT: rebuilding the world economy
notes.b: Alongside regional recovery, the Western powers rebuilt the rules of world money and trade. Their aim was stable exchange rates and falling tariffs, the opposite of the inter-war chaos.
points: The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 created the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. It fixed currencies to the US dollar, which was convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce.

The fixed exchange rate system gave Western economies stable conditions for trade and investment, because firms could trade without fearing sudden currency swings. It lasted until the strains of the 1960s undermined it.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was signed at Geneva on 30 October 1947 by 23 states and came into force on 1 January 1948. It provided a framework for reducing tariffs through successive rounds of negotiation.
The GATT rounds, including the Kennedy Round (talks 1964–67, concluded 1967), reduced tariffs on industrial goods across the Western world.

In December 1958 the main Western European currencies became convertible, which meant they could be freely exchanged for dollars. This ended the controls on trade payments that had survived from the war.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: Bretton Woods (1944, money), GATT (1947, trade) and the 1971 breakdown.

notes.h: Moves towards free trade in Western Europe
notes.b: Within Western Europe, states went further than GATT by forming trading blocs. Each one lowered barriers between its members in a different way.
points: The Benelux customs union (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) was agreed by a convention signed in London in 1944 and began operating on 1 January 1948. A customs union removes tariffs between members and sets a common tariff against outsiders.
The European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) was created by the Treaty of Paris in 1951 and came into force in 1952. It covered trade in coal and steel only.

The European Economic Community (EEC) was created by the Treaty of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957 and in force from 1 January 1958. Its six members were Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

The EEC abolished internal industrial tariffs on 1 July 1968, 18 months early, and had the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) in operation from 1962. The CAP set common farm prices, so the 1968 date relates to industrial tariffs and common farm prices, not the start of the CAP.

The European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was set up by the Stockholm Convention of 1960. Its members were Britain, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal. They removed tariffs on industrial goods, but not on farm produce, and had no common external tariff.
notes.tip: Keep ECSC (1952), EEC (1958), EFTA (1960) and Benelux (1948) apart, and say what each did for trade. The politics of unity is a different question, so focus on trade effects.

notes.b: West Germany's recovery was so rapid that it became known as an economic miracle. Reform of money and prices released the market, and a distinctive economic model kept it stable.
points: The currency reform of 20 June 1948 introduced the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones. It was an Allied measure, not a German one, and it restored confidence in money.
Days later Ludwig Erhard, then director of economic administration, ended most price controls. He was economics minister from 1949 to 1963. Do not confuse him with Adenauer, who was chancellor.
Erhard's social market economy combined free markets with social insurance and trade union rights, so it gave West Germany a stable framework.
Together these reforms created the basis of the economic miracle, the Wirtschaftswunder.
West Germany's economy grew at more than 7 per cent a year on average in the 1950s. Unemployment was about 1.3 per cent in 1960 and under 1 per cent from 1961.
notes.tip: Credit the currency reform to the Allies and the end of price controls to Erhard. Unemployment was about 1.3 per cent in 1960, so say under 1 per cent only from 1961.

notes.h: Growth in France and Italy, and what the boom had in common
notes.b: France and Italy also grew rapidly but in different ways: France through state planning and Italy through industry and the movement of labour. Britain, by contrast, grew more slowly.
points: In France the state planning system began with the Monnet Plan of 1946–47, led by the Commissariat général du Plan. Its priorities were coal, electricity, steel, cement, transport and farm machinery.
The Commissariat set targets for key industries through successive national plans. The state also owned key firms, so Renault was nationalised in 1945.
The French economy grew strongly through the 1950s and 1960s. The economist Jean Fourastié later coined the name trente glorieuses (the thirty glorious years, covering about 1945–75).

Italy's boom ran roughly from 1958 to 1963 and was built on exports of Fiat cars, domestic appliances and textiles. The south (the Mezzogiorno) stayed poor, so many people moved to Turin, Milan and abroad, straining housing and services in the north.
Britain grew more slowly than the continental economies, and balance-of-payments crises produced stop-go policy (swings between expansion and restraint).

Common features were reconstruction, catching up with American methods, cheap oil from the Middle East, skilled and mobile labour, rising exports and rising domestic demand. The adoption of American production methods and the reintegration of trade sustained productivity growth.
notes.tip: Keep the three booms apart: Wirtschaftswunder (West Germany), trente glorieuses (France) and the Italian miracle.

notes.h: Labour shortages and guest workers in West Germany
notes.b: Fast growth created more jobs than local workers could fill, so Western Europe turned to workers from abroad. West Germany's guest worker system is the clearest example.
points: Labour was short for several reasons. The war had killed many working-age men, growth created many new jobs, and rising education and living standards meant fewer locals wanted low-paid, heavy or dirty work.
West Germany recruited guest workers, the Gastarbeiter, under agreements with Italy in 1955, Spain and Greece in 1960, Turkey in 1961 and Yugoslavia in 1968.
Until the Berlin Wall was built in August 1961, workers had also come from East Germany. Once the Wall ended that flow, guest workers became more important to West German industry.
Recruitment was halted in November 1973, by which time there were well over two million foreign workers.
Many guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and their families joined them, which made Western Europe multicultural in the later decades.
notes.tip: For guest workers, give who, where, why and when it stopped: Italy 1955 to Yugoslavia 1968, labour shortages, and the halt of 1973.

notes.h: Immigration to France, Britain and elsewhere
notes.b: France and Britain drew many workers from their former empires, who often had citizenship or settlement rights, unlike temporary guest workers. This brought economic benefits and also social tensions.
points: France drew workers from its former colonies in North Africa (Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia) and from Portugal, and Belgium from Italy and Spain. They worked in construction and car factories.
Algeria became independent in 1962, and several hundred thousand pieds-noirs (settlers of European origin) moved to France.

Britain admitted workers from the Commonwealth. The arrival of the Empire Windrush at Tilbury on 22 June 1948, with over 1,000 passengers, several hundred of them from the Caribbean, marked a major stage in Commonwealth migration.
The British Nationality Act of 1948 gave Commonwealth citizens the right to enter and settle in Britain. The Commonwealth Immigrants Acts of 1962 and 1968 restricted this right.
Commonwealth migrants from the Caribbean, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh worked in the NHS, transport and textile factories. They faced discrimination in housing and employment.
Immigration brought social tensions, and the Race Relations Act of 1965 was Britain's first law against racial discrimination in public places.
The Netherlands received migrants from Indonesia, its former colony, from 1945 onwards, and Italy and Spain exported workers to northern Europe.
Overall, migrants brought economic benefit by filling jobs and supporting growth, but they met discrimination and caused housing pressure. Settled families made the societies multicultural.
notes.tip: Immigration questions reward both benefits and tensions, and naming a specific law or date is credited: the 1948 Act, the 1962 and 1968 restrictions and the 1965 Race Relations Act.

notes.b: The welfare state gave citizens protection against sickness, unemployment and old age.
points: The Beveridge Report of December 1942, by Sir William Beveridge, identified five giant evils: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. It proposed a system of national insurance, in which workers pay contributions to get benefits.
Clement Attlee was prime minister from 1945 to 1951. His Labour government passed the National Insurance Act of 1946.
Britain's National Health Service (NHS) was founded on 5 July 1948 by Aneurin Bevan, the minister of health, and provided free treatment at the point of use.
Attlee's government also nationalised the Bank of England (1946), coal (1947) and the railways (1948).
The Education Act of 1944 made secondary education free, and universities grew in the 1960s.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Beveridge (a Liberal who wrote the report), Attlee (Labour prime minister who implemented it) and Bevan (minister of health who created the NHS).

notes.h: The welfare state in other countries and the post-war consensus
notes.b: Other Western European states built their own welfare systems, often from older traditions. Welfare was accepted by parties of left and right, so it grew steadily.
points: France's social security system was created by ordinances of October 1945. It combined health insurance, family allowances and pensions for workers.

West Germany's welfare system was closely tied to the social market economy. Social insurance dates from Bismarck's laws of the 1880s and was revived, and it provided compulsory insurance funded by employers and employees.

The Scandinavian countries developed universal welfare systems, meaning benefits for all citizens. In Sweden, Social Democratic governments from the 1930s to the 1970s combined social security with active labour market policies.
Christian Democratic governments in West Germany, Italy and Belgium also supported social insurance, which showed that the welfare state was favoured by parties of both left and right.
Welfare spending rose steadily across Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, and it became a permanent feature of the political consensus.
notes.tip: Welfare questions ask you to contrast Britain, France, Germany and Scandinavia, and to mention the cross-party consensus.

notes.h: Factors that helped and hindered growth
notes.b: The boom had many causes, and some things also slowed it. Group the factors by type, such as state action, foreign aid and trade, and labour and energy, then judge which mattered most.
points: Helped, investment and labour: high investment in industry, the move of workers from farms into factories in Italy, France and West Germany, and the supply of labour from refugees and later guest workers.
Helped, energy and technology: access to cheap oil, which kept factory costs low, and the catching up with American technology and management methods.
Helped, trade and aid: Marshall Aid, freer trade and growing export markets, because exports paid for imports and gave factories steady demand.
Helped, state action: governments accepted responsibility for full employment, using the ideas of John Maynard Keynes to manage demand, and political stability supported long-term investment.
Helped, war: the Korean War boom of 1950–53 raised demand for European exports of steel and machinery.
Hindered, early: war damage, which cut output, and the shortage of dollars in the late 1940s, and the cost of rearmament and Cold War defence spending.
Hindered, Britain: weak productivity and frequent strikes, and balance-of-payments crises that led governments to alternate between expansion and restraint, known as stop-go policies.
Hindered, late 1960s: inflation and pressure on currencies as wages rose, and Vietnam War spending and American deficits, which weakened the dollar.
notes.tip: This is the commonest Higher essay. Group factors (state action, foreign aid and trade, labour and energy), give dated examples and judge which mattered most, because a list without explanation scores poorly.

notes.h: Assessment: why did the boom end?
notes.b: The boom of 1945–1973 is judged as the most prosperous period in Western Europe's modern history, but its causes and its end are debated. Weigh achievements against limits.
points: Achievements: unprecedented growth, rising living standards, full employment in many countries, welfare provision, the spread of home ownership and a large expansion of education.
Limits: dependence on cheap oil and on the dollar-based system, inflation in the late 1960s, uneven growth (Britain, southern Italy) and the difficult position of migrants.

The Bretton Woods system broke down after US president Richard Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold on 15 August 1971, and by early 1973 currencies were floating (their values set by the market).
Western Europe's growth rate between 1950 and 1973 was far higher than in any earlier period, but it slowed sharply after 1973 (see the notes on the Oil Crisis).
Historians disagree on how far Marshall Aid caused recovery. Some stress American aid and pressure for cooperation, while Milward and others stress domestic policy and economic structure.
Contemporaries saw the boom as the result of good management. Later historians stress that it was partly a catching-up with the American economy that could not continue indefinitely.
notes.tip: Pair strengths (growth, employment, welfare) with weaknesses (inflation, oil dependence, regional gaps, discrimination against migrants). A single paragraph on the 1971 collapse of Bretton Woods earns credit when linking to the Oil Crisis.

keyTerms.definition: A system in which the state provides health care, pensions, unemployment benefit and education to citizens, funded mainly through taxation and insurance.
An economic system in which private owners run businesses for profit in competitive markets, which the Western economies relied on after 1945.
A trading area in which goods, services, capital and workers move freely between member states, with common external tariffs.
The US aid programme of 1948 to 1952 that provided about 13 billion dollars to help Western European recovery.
The 1944 monetary order that fixed currencies to the US dollar, which was convertible into gold, and created the IMF and the World Bank.
A foreign worker recruited under an agreement for temporary work in a Western European economy, often in West Germany.
Ludwig Erhard's model for West Germany, combining free markets with social insurance and trade union rights.
The West German economic miracle of the 1950s, when rapid growth followed the 1948 currency reform and Erhard's market policies.
The thirty years of rapid growth in France between 1945 and 1975.

keyTerms.term: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
keyTerms.definition: The 1947 agreement under which states met in rounds of talks to reduce tariffs and barriers to trade.
